statement: enforcer-scan (arc-15) already fully implements the tri-modal scope resolver (enforcer_scan::scope::{ScopeRequest,resolve}) with Windows-first normalization and a real ArgGroup-shaped 'exactly one mode' invariant baked into the type -- arc-22 does NOT need to reimplement scope parsing/resolution logic, only bridge clap's parsed ScopeArgs into a ScopeRequest and let enforcer_scan::scope::resolve do the real work. The only gap: enforcer_scan::walk::walk(root, rules) walks the WHOLE tree from a root Path and ignores ResolvedScope::explicit_paths/diff_range entirely -- for Paths-mode scope the CLI must itself filter the walked file list by prefix-match against explicit_paths, and for Diff-mode there is no git-diff-range narrowing anywhere in enforcer-scan yet (the CLI's Diff mode currently walks and scans the FULL tree, not just the diff range, which is a real functional gap a later pack should close, not something arc-22 can silently paper over).
why: A worker skimming only enforcer_scan's module docs (which describe walk as part of the tri-modal contract) could assume walk already narrows by scope and wire check/verify naively, producing a CLI that silently scans everything on every invocation regardless of --base/--head, with no test catching it because the fixture happens to be small.
howToApply: When wiring any CLI/engine caller onto enforcer_scan::{scope,walk,engine}, always trace resolve() -> walk() -> engine::run() end to end for EACH of the three ScopeRequest variants and confirm the file list actually narrows for Paths and (if claimed) Diff mode, not just that the ResolvedScope::kind discriminant is correct.

evidence.ref: crates/enforcer-scan/src/walk.rs pub fn walk(root: &Path, ...) ignores ResolvedScope; crates/enforcer-cli/src/commands.rs resolve_files() adds the prefix-filter for Paths mode and documents the unresolved Diff-mode gap

statement: clap's ArgGroup semantics for a 'both these args together form one logical mode, distinct from these other args' shape needs TWO separate ArgGroup declarations, not one: a group over {base,head} declared with .multiple(true) (both members may be set simultaneously, since --base/--head are a pair) PLUS a separate 'scope' group over {paths,all} with .multiple(false).conflicts_with("base_head") referencing the first group's NAME. Declaring only .conflicts_with on an implicit group name (one only ever referenced via #[arg(group="base_head")] attrs, never explicitly ArgGroup::new'd) silently no-ops the requires="head"/requires="base" pairing check AND rejects a legitimate --base X --head Y invocation as an internal group-multiplicity conflict.
why: The failure mode is subtle: `cargo test` shows check_with_base_head_parses failing with ArgumentConflict (not a clean parse error) and base_without_head_is_a_clap_error failing because parsing UNEXPECTEDLY SUCCEEDS -- both point at the group's own multiplicity default (false) silently swallowing the requires= pairing rather than at the conflicts_with target being wrong, which is the intuitive place to look first.
howToApply: For any 'these N args are jointly one mode, mutually exclusive with that other mode' clap grammar, always explicitly ArgGroup::new declare EVERY group referenced by name (never rely on an attribute-only implicit group), and set .multiple(true) on any group whose members can/must co-occur (like a base+head pair) before wiring a .conflicts_with from a different group.

evidence.ref: crates/enforcer-cli/src/cli.rs ScopeArgs -- first pass had only #[arg(group="base_head")] attrs with no ArgGroup::new("base_head"), fixed by adding ArgGroup::new("base_head").args(["base","head"]).multiple(true)

statement: enforcer-mcp (arc-21) already exposes the exact entry point enforcer-cli's `serve` subcommand needs: enforcer_mcp::sink::run_stdio_server(&DispatchContext) plus enforcer_mcp::sink::default_dispatch_context(cli_path). arc-21's own src/bin/enforcer-mcp-smoke.rs is explicitly documented in its own module doc as a THROWAWAY harness that calls this exact same public entry point 'solely because enforcer-cli (arc-22) didn't exist yet' -- once arc-22 lands `serve`, that smoke binary becomes redundant (its own proof and arc-22's live serve+initialize proof now cover identical code paths) but it is NOT owned by arc-22 (owns: crates/enforcer-mcp/**) and must not be deleted by this lane.
why: A future cleanup pass or a worker skimming file lists could either (a) leave the now-redundant smoke binary indefinitely out of caution, duplicating proof coverage forever, or (b) delete it out-of-scope and break arc-21's own already-landed P3 proof row (tests/stdio_smoke.rs depends on it existing).
howToApply: Flag (do not act on) cross-crate redundancy discovered while landing a dependent pack; the owning crate's maintainers decide removal timing against their own proof rows, never the downstream consumer that discovers the redundancy.

evidence.ref: crates/enforcer-mcp/src/bin/enforcer-mcp-smoke.rs module doc 'Ownership note'; crates/enforcer-mcp/tests/stdio_smoke.rs depends on the binary existing

statement: The 'architecture-policy' named check referenced by the workpack's orphaned-subcommand port request has NO backing Rust validator anywhere in the workspace as of arc-22 -- it exists ONLY as a string literal in enforcer-mcp's NAMED_CHECKS parity table (crates/enforcer-mcp/src/registry.rs), which is bookkeeping for future check-enum parity, not a runnable engine. Its sibling 'import-boundaries' DOES have a real landed validator (enforcer_lang_ts::rules::import_boundaries::ImportBoundariesValidator). arc-22's `architecture check --language rust` therefore cannot honestly report a clean/dirty verdict for architecture-policy and instead reports the gap through the InternalError exit class with a diagnostic naming it explicitly, rather than silently returning '0 findings, clean' for a check that does not actually run.
why: Silently mapping an unimplemented named check to a clean Report would be indistinguishable from the check having actually run and found nothing -- exactly the 'CI misreads an enforcer gap as project health' failure the exit-code-taxonomy requirement is designed to prevent, just at the named-check granularity instead of the process-crash granularity.
howToApply: Before wiring ANY CLI subcommand onto a 'named check' string, grep for its actual backing Validator/engine function across crates/, not just its presence in a registry/enum string table -- a name existing in a parity table is not evidence a runnable implementation exists.

evidence.ref: crates/enforcer-mcp/src/registry.rs NAMED_CHECKS array (string only); crates/enforcer-lang-ts/src/rules/import_boundaries.rs (real validator); crates/enforcer-cli/src/commands.rs run_architecture_check() Rust arm

statement: arc-22's checkpoint (pass 1) had a real exit-code-taxonomy bug that its own test suite did not catch: main.rs's run() mapped EVERY clap::Error from Cli::try_parse() (including --help and --version, which clap deliberately routes through the Err branch by design so callers control the exit) into ExitCode::UsageError (2). --help/--version therefore exited 2 instead of 0 on the REAL compiled binary, even though every existing unit/integration test asserted only stdout TEXT content (e.g. help_never_advertises_a_bypass_flag checked .output().stdout, never .status()), so 49/49 tests stayed green while the live binary was wrong. Fixed by branching on clap::Error::use_stderr() (false for DisplayHelp/DisplayVersion-kind errors, true for genuine parse failures) instead of treating the whole Err arm as one exit class.
why: A CI wrapper that runs `enforcer --version` to log the binary's identity (a very ordinary CI pattern) would have seen exit code 2 and could misinterpret that as a usage/config problem in ITS OWN invocation, exactly the ambiguity the exit-code taxonomy requirement exists to prevent -- and no existing test would have caught it because none of the clap-Err-path tests asserted process exit code, only rendered text.
howToApply: When any CLI grammar's top-level parse-error handling maps clap::Error to a custom exit-code enum, always branch on err.use_stderr() (or equivalently err.kind()) to separate DisplayHelp/DisplayVersion/DisplayHelpOnMissingArgumentOrSubcommand from real usage errors -- and write at least one test per lane that asserts the PROCESS EXIT CODE of --help/--version on the real compiled binary, not just its stdout text, since text-only assertions cannot catch an exit-code miscoercion.

evidence.ref: crates/enforcer-cli/src/main.rs run() -- `./target/debug/enforcer.exe --help` measured exit code 2 before the fix, 0 after; fixed via err.use_stderr() branch

statement: A naive `text.contains("serve")` substring assertion against clap-rendered --help output is NOT a safe way to prove a subcommand is absent: the `install` subcommand's own help prose ('this skeleton only reserves the subcommand name...') contains the literal substring 'serve' inside the word 'reserves', so the assertion false-failed against a CORRECTLY-built lite binary that genuinely had no serve/coordination/ledger subcommands. The fix matches the exact two-space-indented `Commands:` listing line clap renders per subcommand ('  serve ' or '  serve\n'), not a bare substring, to distinguish 'the subcommand is listed' from 'the word appears anywhere in any subcommand's prose'.
why: This is a general trap for any CLI proof that greps rendered help/usage text for a word that also happens to be a common English substring (serve/reserve, ci/police, plan/planner, etc.) -- the assertion can fail on a correct binary (false negative on correctness) just as easily as it can silently pass on a broken one (false positive on correctness), and both failure directions look identical in a CI log ('test failed') without inspecting the actual --help text.
howToApply: When asserting a CLI subcommand's absence/presence from rendered --help text, always anchor the match to the renderer's own line shape (leading indent + exact name + trailing space/newline, matching clap's `Commands:` block format) rather than a bare substring search; when a substring assertion fails unexpectedly, print/inspect the full captured text before concluding the binary (not the test) is wrong.

evidence.ref: crates/enforcer-cli/tests/cli_integration.rs lite_help_omits_full_only_subcommands -- first version used text.contains("serve") and failed against a correctly-built lite binary due to the word 'reserves' in the install subcommand's own help string
